item.title: Signs point to renewed major U.S. military operations against Iran
item.description:
The United States appears to be preparing to resume large-scale strikes against Iran, but there is unlikely to be a military solution for either side in the devastating conflict, experts say.

Washington and Tehran's forces have settled into a pattern of strikes on commercial ships, with the United States seeking to enforce a blockade of Iran's ports and the Islamic republic trying to exert control over the key Strait of Hormuz waterway.

Neither country has engaged in major attacks on land-based targets since early September, but that may soon change.

"I'm banking now on the likelihood of strikes shortly after the midterms," said Suzanne Maloney, director of the foreign policy program at the Brookings Institution, referring to November 3 elections in the United States.

She pointed to potential signs including the movement of additional US military assets and troops to the Middle East, warnings issued to Americans in the region, and a high alert status for Israeli forces.

Additionally, President Donald Trump "came out publicly and said that he wouldn't strike before the midterms," and "it wouldn't seem to help him at the polls to do so," Maloney said.

The US-Israeli war against Iran is largely unpopular in the United States, especially because it has sharply driven up fuel prices, and is likely to be a drag on Trump's Republican Party in the key vote.

"Fundamentally, the situation isn't sustainable in its current state," Maloney said, noting that the US blockade is "creating greater pain for the Iranians," while Washington has a large number of naval assets tied up in enforcing it.

Trump said Friday that "we may do another little Epic Fury" -- the name for the US operation against Iran that was launched in late February -- if Tehran does not make a deal, but gave no indication on timing.

- 'Impossible to predict' -

Jason Campbell, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, said there have "certainly been recent signs that renewed strikes may be in the offing," or that "the US is expecting strikes carried out by Iran" or their Houthi allies in Yemen.

He noted the planned deployment of the USS Theodore Roosevelt to the Middle East -- which could at least temporarily bring the number of carrier strike groups there to three -- as well as the decision to dispatch another Marine Expeditionary Unit to the region.

Campbell also said Israeli warplanes recently carried out a "show of force" mimicking previous strikes on Iran, and noted that US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Israel.

However, "timing here is impossible to predict," he said of renewed strikes, while noting that "this is admittedly an expansive set of actions to take if the intent is to simply pressure Iran to the negotiating table."

Campbell said Trump's options are more limited than they were earlier in the conflict, with damage to US bases in the region having made any potential ground operation more difficult.

"At this point, there is no safe place to stage the thousands (in some scenarios tens of thousands) of forces that would be required for such an operation," he said.

Maloney meanwhile said that "most of the conventional military sites (in Iran) have already been heavily degraded" by previous strikes, meaning any new campaign will likely "entail more strikes on civilian infrastructure and targets that impact the Iranian population."

But that -- or any type of military action -- is unlikely to bring about a resolution to the conflict.

"From the start... this has been a war that can't be ended with further escalation on either side," Maloney said.

Campbell agreed, saying: "I do not see how renewed strikes on Iran akin to the first fifty days of the war will move the strategic needle for the Iranian regime."

"They have demonstrated a willingness to absorb a significant amount of physical pain and even some alterations to targeting that includes key mixed or even civilian infrastructure will not significantly change this," he added.

wd/sms

This article originally appeared on AFP at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/signs-point-renewed-major-us-175157103.html

item.title: Musk says he was behind Starlink disruptions, claiming Ukraine service violations
item.description:
KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Elon Musk said on Saturday that his company SpaceX had throttled the Starlink satellite internet service in Ukraine, disrupting operations that the country relies on to defend itself against Russia.

Musk's admission on social media came after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Ukraine’s access to Starlink and Starshield satellite links has been restored to the speeds it had before restrictions that disrupted front-line operations for more than a week.

Questions have persisted since last week about who ordered the interruptions to the Musk-made satellite internet system that Kyiv has relied on for years to counter Moscow’s attacks.

“The speeds are now where they need to be,” Zelenskyy wrote on X, adding that restoration began overnight and were sufficient by Saturday morning, improving front-line logistics and defense against Russian jet-powered Shahed drones.

Musk admits he was behind Starlink’s speed restriction

After Ukraine said the services had been restored, Elon Musk spoke out on the speed restrictions that began last week. In a post Saturday on X, Musk acknowledged that his company SpaceX throttled the Starlink satellite internet service.

“Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be,” Musk wrote. “Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week.”

But he maintained that the U.S. government controlled whatever changes happened with Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink that is the backbone of Ukraine’s drone operations and communication. He also defended the role of SpaceX in bolstering Ukraine’s defenses since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Restrictions imposed last week on Starshield alarmed the country’s military and government officials, with commanders reporting lost drones and disrupted missions.

The restoration follows a new U.S. diplomatic push to end the war. Russia agreed Wednesday to resume three-way negotiations with Washington and Kyiv next month. On Friday, Kyiv and Moscow also agreed to a localized ceasefire brokered by first lady Melania Trump around Oleshky, a war-ravaged, Russian-occupied town in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region.

Restriction led to tensions between Ukraine and the US

The episode added to tensions between Kyiv and Washington, a relationship already strained by President Donald Trump’s reported deal with Moscow on Russian diesel imports, which Ukraine viewed as a betrayal.

Ukraine's Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara credited “direct dialogue” and Zelenskyy’s diplomacy with Washington, adding that the outcome mattered most “for our front, for the military, the work of drones, logistics and communications.”

Trump has maintained that he didn’t make the call, while also saying Musk should not be blamed. Vice President JD Vance has hinted at White House coordination with Musk, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth have denied any administration involvement.

Russia and Ukraine have continued to target each other

Meanwhile, a man was killed and two others wounded in a missile attack on the city of Lozova in Ukraine's Kharkiv region, local officials said Saturday.

Moscow-installed authorities in cities across Russia-occupied Crimea reported power blackouts Saturday following overnight Ukrainian attacks.

Ukraine’s General Staff said Saturday that its forces hit a chemical plant in the Russian city of Tolyatti, which produces materials used in rocket fuel. Tolyatti Mayor Ilya Sukhikh said the overnight attack damaged industrial facilities in the city.

Ukrainian forces also hit an electronics plant in the city of Oryol, Ukraine’s General Staff confirmed Saturday. Local officials in Oryol said Saturday that three people were killed in Friday’s attack. The General Staff said the plant makes components for the cruise and ballistic missiles Russia fires at Ukrainian cities.

Ukrainian drones also reached Russia’s Omsk region in western Siberia, more than 2,000 kilometers (1,242 miles) from the border with Ukraine. Omsk regional Gov. Vitaly Khotsenko said drones “reached a northern industrial hub.”

Online retailer Ozon said Saturday that its logistics center in Omsk has been attacked by a drone, but there were no casualties. Ozon is a competitor to Wildberries, whose facilities Ukraine has also targeted.

___

Morton reported from London.

___

Follow the AP’s coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine

item.title: 'Weaponizing the law': California AG slams DOJ's attack on alleged noncitizen voting
item.description:
California’s attorney general on Saturday rebuked the Trump administration’s efforts to quash alleged noncitizen voting, calling it “politicizing and weaponizing the law”.

Rob Bonta, the state’s attorney general, said the justice department acted at Donald Trump’s direction.

“It is once again the United States Department of Justice politicizing and weaponizing the law to attack its enemies, and it is completely improper,” he told MS Now.

Less than two weeks before the midterms, federal prosecutors called upon California election officials to verify within 48 hours a list of about 20,000 ballots belonging to suspected noncitizens. Noncitizen voting is extremely rare, but in the run-up to the midterm elections, the justice department has ramped up prosecutions of people accused of illegally voting while not holding US citizenship.

California’s election personnel have raised concern that the administration’s directive could disenfranchise citizens. Los Angeles officials said this week a “high percentage” of the individuals on the list were born in the United States.

“Trump’s DOJ is so desperate to invent ‘widespread voter fraud,’ it sent California counties lists of people who NEVER voted – and voters from the WRONG COUNTY. Absolute clown show!” California’s governor Gavin Newsom posted on social media.

“Voter intimidation has no place in our democracy,” Pete Aguilar, a congressman representing south-west San Bernardino county, said in a social media post.

The federal government’s oversight attempts come amid a national Republican effort to crack down on alleged voter fraud, particularly any cases among undocumented immigrants.

“We are asking each county election official to commit to working with us by providing the necessary information for DHS to quickly verify citizenship status. With their help, we can ensure the most secure election in California history,” the justice department said.

Bonta, the California attorney general, has raised questions about the evidence behind the suspected noncitizen ballots.

“All they provided was a list of people and nothing about why they’re purportedly ineligible. If they have such information, we would be happy to review it, but they’ve provided none,” Bonta said at a recent press conference.

The DoJ also charged 28 foreign nationals recently, accusing them of fraudulently registering to vote.

“Today’s arrests prove what we have been saying,” Bill Essayli, first assistant US attorney, said in a statement. “California is mailing ballots to noncitizens, and they are refusing to comply with federal law, which makes it a crime for noncitizens to vote. The voting rights of American citizens must be protected.”

The defendants are lawful permanent residents, who have legal status in the US but are not citizens authorized to vote.

Some state officials took no action on Friday’s letters, citing the fast-approaching election, which spurred a legal battle with the justice department. An appeals court is set to hear the matter on Tuesday.

This article originally appeared on The Guardian at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/california-leaders-rebuke-trump-administration-001617824.html

item.title: Nearly 1,000 arrested in French protests marred by 'extremely elevated' violence
item.description:
French police arrested "nearly 1,000" people Saturday in nationwide protests in which officers were confronted with "an extremely elevated level of violence" from black-clad extremists, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said.

Although marches over the cost of living "passed off well" in cities, "ultra-left" groups took to throwing projectiles and aiming fireworks at police to provoke clashes, he told journalists.

Two people were "seriously injured", he said: one in the city of Toulouse, where a 20-year-old man reportedly had fingers blown off, and the other in Clermont-Ferrand. He did not give details of either case.

Nunez compared Saturday's figures with those from a week ago, when a first round of national demonstrations over the cost of living degenerated into street violence, with hundreds of shops looted and 2,700 people ending up being arrested.

He said that the nearly 1,000 arrests recorded on Saturday compared with the same time a week ago, when authorities had recorded 385 arrests.

He also said that, while some shops and businesses had been vandalised and looted on Saturday, "the scale was far smaller" than a week earlier, and he stressed that shopping centres had been well protected this time.

In Paris, where the main demonstration passed off largely peacefully but clashes broke out with police as the crowd dispersed, Nunez said "several thousand radical activists gathered at the rear of the march, including around 500 individuals identified as rioters".

Ensuing clashes in the capital lasted for around two hours, he said.

The minister said that in the southern cities of Cannes and Montpellier, authorities "for the first time" saw far-right activists who sought confrontations with "ultra-left militants" or who claimed to be there to protect businesses.

Overall, Nunez said, Saturday's outcome appeared more "positive" than a week ago, with more police on the streets acting more rapidly, conducting more pre-demonstration checks and better protecting businesses.

The authorities would remain "on high alert" through the night and into Sunday, he said.

item.title: Brazil's tight runoff tests Trump officials' bid to bring Bolsonaros back to power
item.description:
By Gabriel Stargardter

SAO PAULO, Oct 24 (Reuters) - Two US State Department officials led a campaign to restore the right-wing Bolsonaro clan to power in Brazil and successfully pushed for sanctions aimed at tilting the election in their favor, according to 10 current and former US officials with direct knowledge of the matter.

Their plan faces a reckoning on Sunday, when Senator Flavio Bolsonaro faces leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in a tight run-off. Lula has warned Washington against encroaching on Brazil's sovereignty and accused his opponent of plotting with the Trump administration.

The two officials were Darren Beattie, a Senior Advisor ‌for Western Hemisphere Affairs who oversees Brazil policy, and Ricardo Pita, another senior advisor promoted this year to Deputy Assistant Secretary for North America. The details of their campaign to return the Bolsonaros to power haven't been previously reported.

Beattie and Pita, both political appointees, operated with wide latitude to manage Washington's relationship with the ‌second most-populous country in the Americas, the people said.

In the months before election campaigning began, they instructed US diplomats in Brazil that it was US policy to restore former President Jair Bolsonaro as Brazil’s leader – even though he had been disqualified from office for plotting a coup in 2022, when he lost the presidential election to Lula, three of the people said.

After Bolsonaro received a 27-year sentence in September 2025, the two men pivoted to ​supporting the candidacy of his son, right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the three sources said. Beattie and Pita told embassy staff not to interact with other conservative presidential contenders who could challenge the younger Bolsonaro, they said.

Since last year, the two men have successfully advocated for punitive US government measures on Brazil designed to weaken Lula and boost the Bolsonaros, the 10 people told Reuters. The policies included designating Brazilian gangs as terrorist groups and imposing US sanctions against the Brazilian Supreme Court Justice who was spearheading the investigation into Jair Bolsonaro.

Reuters could not determine the extent to which the two men were acting on orders from the White House or Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Trump, a vocal defender of Bolsonaro since his election defeat in 2022, hasn’t publicly endorsed any candidate.

The White House declined to comment and referred questions to the State Department.

State Department Spokesman Tommy Pigott didn't answer questions about specific measures and directives involving Beattie and Pita but said in a statement: "All actions taken by the United States against narco-traffickers and to protect free speech are to defend the rights and lives of the American people. The Brazilian people have the right to ‌choose their leaders through free and fair elections."

Lula’s office did not respond to comment requests.

Orna Blum, one of the officials who ⁠spoke to Reuters about Beattie and Pita’s efforts, led the State Department's Brazil and Southern Cone office until retiring last year over her opposition to the Trump administration.

Washington "has every right to pursue its economic and strategic interests," she said. "But when American foreign policy instruments are used to pressure another democracy over the legal fate of a political ally, the line between diplomacy and political intervention has been crossed."

SANCTIONS ON A SUPREME COURT JUSTICE

Beattie is a former White House speechwriter fired in 2018 after addressing an event frequented by white nationalists. He’s also the architect of "free speech ⁠diplomacy," a policy advocated by Trump allies that seeks to punish nations they accuse of censoring right-wing speech by US citizens, companies and global right-wing allies.

The United States has accused Brazil Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes of violating free speech rights by jailing Brazilians for political social-media posts and by censoring content of US social-media companies. Moraes has argued he was ridding social media of fake news that undermined public faith in Brazil's democratic institutions.

Moraes did not respond to a comment request.

Pita, a conservative Venezuelan-American, is among many in Rubio's orbit who view Lula as a threat to US interests in Latin America. Rubio has been a key leader in the administration’s aggressive policy in the region, which has included an invasion of Venezuela to oust its president, an oil blockade of Cuba, and military attacks ​on suspected ​drug boats from Latin America.

Beattie and Pita were drawn to the Bolsonaro family’s right-wing politics, their antipathy towards Lula, and the idea that Jair Bolsonaro was a victim of abuses by Brazil's Supreme Court.

Like ​Trump in the 2020 US election, Bolsonaro refused to concede he lost Brazil’s 2022 presidential vote, triggering riots by supporters who stormed government ‌buildings. The Supreme Court convicted him in September 2025 of plotting a coup to remain in power.

Before the conviction, in early 2025, the Bolsonaros were aggressively lobbying Washington for sanctions under the Global Magnitsky Human Rights Accountability Act against Moraes, who had led criminal investigations into Jair Bolsonaro. The act is a 2016 federal law allowing US sanctions against foreign individuals responsible for human-rights abuses or severe corruption.

Around April 2025, Jair Bolsonaro’s younger son, Eduardo, visited Beattie in his State Department office in Washington DC, according to two former US officials. Eduardo Bolsonaro had been making the public case for Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes since at least 2024, and in March 2025 he said in a livestream that it was "practically certain" the Trump administration would do so.

Eduardo Bolsonaro did not respond to requests for comment.

Beattie made calls to the US Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control to appeal for Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes, said a former US official with direct knowledge of the matter.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, whose department administers Magnitsky sanctions through OFAC, offered no opposition, the former official said.

The US announced Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes in July 2025, citing his alleged violations of free-speech rights by censoring anti-government social-media posts.

A Treasury official said Bessent and Rubio are "fully aligned on the administration’s foreign policy."

TERRORIST DESIGNATIONS

The Bolsonaro family was also pushing for Washington to designate Brazil's top gangs – the Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC) and Comando Vermelho (CV) – as terrorist organizations. They believed such a designation would hurt Lula, ‌who some opponents have criticized for failing to control crime.

Eduardo Bolsonaro had become friends with Pita through US conservative circles, and both supported the effort to designate the gangs as terrorist groups.

In May 2025, ​Pita joined a US delegation that visited Jair Bolsonaro at his residence in Brasilia as he awaited his trial, according to public announcements at the time. Also in the group: David Gamble, the State Department’s top sanctions ​official at the time.

Back in Washington, Pita asked State sanctions officials to explore how terrorist designations like those announced against Mexican cartels in February 2025 could be used ​in Brazil, one former official said.

Nearly a year later, in May 2026 – after Pita was promoted to a new job that pulled him out of Brazil affairs – presidential contender Flavio Bolsonaro met with Beattie and Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau in Washington to discuss "the urgency of designating the ‌PCC and the Comando Vermelho as foreign terrorist organizations," according to an X post by right-wing influencer Paulo Figueiredo that included ​photos of the attendees.

The State Department announced the designation the following day.

Reuters could not determine the ​extent of Pita or Beattie’s influence in securing the final decision.

BACKFIRES AND SETBACKS

In July 2025, Washington also announced a series of other measures against Brazil, including the revocations of eight Supreme Court justices' visas and 50% tariffs on Brazilian goods, citing the "persecution" of Jair Bolsonaro.

Reuters could not determine what, if any, role Beattie or Pita played in the additional measures. But if they were intended to undermine Lula, many of them backfired, according to political analysts in Brazil.

Measures targeting the court did nothing to stop it from proceeding with Bolsonaro's trial, while the tariffs boosted the Lula government's poll numbers, the analysts said.

Major US and Brazilian firms reliant on bilateral trade – including ​meatpacking giant JBS - controlled by Brazilian billionaires Wesley and Joesley Batista – also pushed back on the tariffs, which Washington eventually watered down.

Beattie ‌and Pita’s campaign also hit setbacks. Without an official explanation from the Treasury Department, the US removed Justice Moraes from the Magnitsky sanctions list in December, and in March Brazil barred Beattie from entering the country to visit Bolsonaro in prison.

Mario Braga, a Latin America analyst at risk intelligence firm RANE, ​said Trump may have decided to withhold a public endorsement of Bolsonaro to avoid being seen as meddling in Brazil's election – a perception that could boost Lula’s popularity.

Still, after Flavio Bolsonaro narrowly outperformed Lula in the first-round election earlier this month, Trump called it a big victory.

"Close, but a very, very ​big victory," he told reporters. "Amazing, actually."

(Reporting by Gabriel StargardterAdditional reporting by Gram Slattery in Washington, Luciana Magalhaes in Sao Paulo, Lisandra Paraguassu in Brasilia Editing by Brad Haynes and Richard Valdmanis)

This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/inside-trump-administration-campaign-return-214506018.html

item.title: Obama rebukes Ramaswamy over Acton ad and hits Trump on costs at Ohio rally
item.description:
In his first rally of the 2026 midterm cycle, former President Barack Obama slammed President Donald Trump and Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, calling out the latter’s much-maligned campaign ad centering on Democrat Amy Acton’s mother.

“There's gotta be something inside you where you just say no office is worth stooping that low,” Obama said of Ramaswamy’s choice to run the ad.

With the midterms just over a week away, Obama was rallying in Cleveland in support of Acton and Democratic Senate candidate Sherrod Brown.

Trump, Obama said, had broken a slew of promises he made on the campaign trail in 2024, ensnaring the country in an ongoing war in Iran and failing to bring down costs. Instead, “he’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory,” the former president said, taking aim at Trump’s renovations to the executive mansion.

“We got two more years of this administration,” he said. “That’s how our system of government works. But you know what we’re not stuck with? We’re not stuck with a spineless Congress and Republican governors who are enabling lawlessness and carelessness and cruelty and indifference for working people.”

Long one of Democrats' top surrogates, Obama is again stepping off the sidelines in the closing stretch of an election. He’ll appear in Detroit alongside Democrats Abdul El-Sayed and Jocelyn Benson on Sunday, after which he’ll travel to Georgia for a rally with Sen. Jon Ossoff and former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms on Oct. 28.

The former president, who captured Ohio’s electoral votes in 2008 and 2012, also called out Ramaswamy for his controversial campaign ad featuring Acton’s mother. Acton was removed from her mother’s home after her stepfather was charged with raping her. She spoke about her childhood in a speech moments before the former president took to the stage on Saturday.

“There's a decency that we should expect out of our public officials,” Obama said. “And I don't know what's happened where the standards of behavior have gotten so low that somebody could run an ad like that.”

The White House and Ramaswamy’s campaign both did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/24/obama-slams-ramaswamy-trump-ohio-rally-midterms-01134765

item.title: Pentagon confirms Hegseth's staff damaged Eisenhower's globe during office move
item.description:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s team dropped and damaged a historic World War II-era globe previously used by Gen. Dwight D. Eisenhower, a source familiar with the incident told The Hill on Thursday.

While moving the artifact to the secretary’s office, Hegseth's staff lost control of the 30-inch floor globe, causing it to crash on its base and resulting in an inches-wide gash near Antarctica, The Washington Post first reported Thursday. 

The Post obtained images of the globe that showed the damage caused during the early February relocation attempt.  

The Army’s press office referred The Hill to Hegseth's office. 

A Pentagon official confirmed to The Hill on Thursday the accident occurred while staff was transporting the replica of the Eisenhower globe as part of its relocation. 

“Accidents happen, we are grateful no one was harmed, and the globe is being repaired,” the official said in a statement. “It is unsurprising that the Washington Post is once again dedicating time to another inconsequential non-story.”

The globe was ultimately not relocated. 

One of the Eisenhower globes has pen lines and markings from World War II on it, the source familiar told The Hill, speaking on condition of anonymity.

Early this year, Hegseth wanted the globe to be relocated to his office, but instead of trained curators, his staff dispatched its own team to do the job, the Post reported.

The Army office in possession of the artifact initially expected to consult with experts to make sure it could be safely transported, the newspaper reported. 

Those plans were later interrupted when staffers were furloughed during a partial government shutdown as a result of a disagreement in Congress over the Trump administration’s immigration policy. After failing to reach the experts, Hegseth’s staff took the matter into its own hands, according to the Post.

The Army's press office referred questions to the Pentagon.

It is unclear whether Hegseth personally asked for the globe to be moved to his office. 

In recent years, another globe, which is around 40 inches in diameter and stands about 4 feet off the ground and is also connected to Eisenhower, was moved from the Army Center of Military History in Anniston, Ala., which is part of the Army Transformation and Training Command, to an Army base. 

“When packing an asset of this size, we had to consider the context of its worth on many levels,” Craters & Freighters wrote in late December 2022. “Since the globe is considered priceless, we knew its value was much greater than financial, and that our team was heavily relied upon for a safe delivery.” 

During World War II, Eisenhower led the attack on Nazi-occupied Europe as supreme commander of the Allied forces, including the D-Day landings in 1944, leading to the liberation of Paris. He later became the 34th U.S. President, serving from 1953 to 1961.

item.title: A Democratic researcher came home to Kansas. Now the GOP faces a Senate fight.
item.description:
Early in September, a New York Times investigation rocked the Kansas Senate race. The incumbent Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, the paper revealed, had sued some 700 patients over his previous, decadeslong career as an obstetrician-gynecologist in rural Kansas; in 81 of the cases, patients had gotten arrested over missed court dates. In an agricultural state already hard-hit by Donald Trump’s tariffs, and in a cycle with affordability as voters’ top issue, the revelation of struggling patients facing legal peril over medical debt — in one case of as little as $101 — changed the map, putting Republicans officially on the defensive in a state that had looked safe only months before.

The story was a coup for the paper and veteran health care reporter Sarah Kliff who, as the paper noted, “reviewed thousands of court records and interviewed eight people whom Roger Marshall sued over medical debt.” But many also suspected a particular hand behind the initial tip: Tyson Brody, a 39-year-old opposition researcher and an alum of both the Hillary Clinton and Bernie Sanders campaigns, who moved home to Kansas to work for Marshall’s Democratic challenger, Rev. Adam Hamilton. Brody is “the kind of guy who, forget a skeleton in your closet — he will find every single dust bunny in your closet,” said Caitlin Legacki, a senior fellow at Third Way and a Democratic strategist who has worked with Brody in the past.

The Times declined to comment, as did both Brody and the Hamilton campaign. Kliff has said on Kansas City public radio that she will not reveal who gave her the tip, as is standard journalistic practice. But journalists and operatives familiar with Brody’s work think it’s no coincidence that the Hamilton campaign’s oppo game is exploding as it happens to employ one of the Democratic party’s top practitioners of the craft — in his own home state.

Marshall has said he treated every patient regardless of ability to pay. But in the weeks since the story ran, polls have tightened, prognosticators have moved the race toward Democrats (the Cook Political report now rates it a toss-up) and millions of dollars have rushed into what suddenly looks like a battleground on the prairie — in a state so associated with conservativism that Democrats use the book title What’s the Matter With Kansas? as shorthand for benighted farmers voting against what liberals see as their own interests. Giddy Democrats and despondent Republicans alike are contemplating the possibility that Kansas could send a Democrat to the Senate for the first time since 1932. And central to that phenomenon — along with a damaged incumbent and a unique challenger — is the old-fashioned, dark art of oppo research.


The dynamics are all the more noteworthy in a fractured media environment where it’s rare for any given story to break through the cacophony of legacy media, newer outlets, online influencers and the attention-sucking machine that is the Donald Trump presidency. But the frenzied competition of the race’s waning days suggests the remaining power of a resonant, records-driven revelation paired with the imprimatur of The New York Times. “It’s a little bit old school,” said Joe Rodota, a former researcher who praised Brody recently on his own Substack, Oppo File. With the caveat that “of course we’ll never know” the origin of the Times story, he said, “I think prior generations of oppo researchers read this story and nod approvingly.”


Which is not to say a Hamilton victory is assured — Kansas has broken Democratic hearts before, including in Marshall’s first Senate campaign in 2020. Then, too, the race featured tightening polls, a moderate, seemingly Kansas-friendly Democratic candidate, and millions rushing into the state in a year expected to be tough for Republicans. In the end, Marshall prevailed by double digits. “We’ve seen this play out before in Kansas,” said Danedri Herbert, who chairs the Kansas GOP.


Still, said Ashley All, a longtime Kansas Democratic operative, “I think it feels different” in 2026. In 2020, for instance, no one had surfaced Marshall’s lawsuits, which were not as easily accessible online at the time. All said that for Democrats to win in the state, they need to run a perfect campaign featuring a near-perfect candidate against a terrible opponent, in a perfect political environment — and then they also need to get lucky. This year, she sees all of those factors — and a strategist who knows how to take advantage of them. “Tyson is obviously operating at a very high level,” she said.


That includes shunning media attention on him personally: He has previously dinged another operative for making himself the story while his candidate was actively campaigning. “I feel like talking about Tyson is itself almost verboten,” said a national Democratic operative who has worked with Brody, granted anonymity to discuss the verboten subject. “He operates in the shadows, which is how most oppo people do.” On the other hand, Brody is all over Twitter pumping out stories likely informed by his own research with strings of incredulous punctuation a la “?????” or “!!!”


Marshall’s campaign, too, is quick to post negative stories about Hamilton — and peddles oppo of its own. “If POLITICO is writing about opposition research in this race, the story is what Kansans have learned about Adam Hamilton in the last three weeks,” wrote Alex DeGrasse, an advisor to Kansans for Marshall, in a statement that included 10 links to stories in conservative outlets. Among them was reporting on a sermon in which Hamilton discussed the benefits of being educated, white and male and said he had to “repent” for his resulting indifference to others’ suffering; that he had donated to and voted for Kamala Harris before asking her not to campaign for him; and that he has made millions off of tech stocks but now calls for slowing down AI development.


DeGrasse also highlighted Hamilton’s recent comments to CNN regarding allegations surfaced by a primary rival that were investigated by local media earlier this year. Hamilton said he wished he’d called the police immediately when allegations of child sexual abuse surfaced at a camp run by his church in 2005 — the victims could not positively identify the perpetrator in the church’s internal investigation, and law enforcement’s investigation was likewise inconclusive when they were notified the next year, according to documents reviewed by the Kansas Reflector. “Kansans can judge for themselves which campaign is running on research and which one is running from it,” DeGrasse wrote.


But GOP operatives have complained to POLITICO that Marshall’s lackluster performance in the race is now costing their party millions to try to save the seat. (Brody duly tweeted out this detail with an “o rly?”) More recently, Marshall has expanded his team with seasoned operatives.


“The oppo has been the kind of stuff that campaign people dream about,” said Legacki. She acknowledged that Brody gets a lot of attention by virtue of being so online. But she also noted that the structure of Hamilton’s campaign allows Brody to function as an attack dog in a way that preserves the candidate’s gentler image as the senior pastor of the United Methodist Church of the Resurrection in Leawood, Kansas. “It’s hard to do that,” she said, “when you’re taking a Midwestern preacher and having him rip a guy’s throat out.”

Brody grew up in Johnson County, Kansas; his father founded the local alt-weekly, The Pitch, in the late 1980s. Brody fils went coastal for college at Columbia, and since then has spent much of his career as a political operative, according to his Substack, which he named “Ragpicker,” after the oppo researcher’s practice of “picking through the refuse of the news cycle.” There, he defines “oppo” as “simply the act of examining a subject’s political, professional, and personal lives, and seeing where the friction lies.”


Ragpicker was active only for a few months in 2025, however; as he wrote, discretion was paramount on campaigns, and by mid-2026 he was back home working for Hamilton — the latest in a line of clients that included Barack Obama in 2012, Clinton in 2016 and Sanders in 2020.This last assignment made minor news, because he’d previously helped assemble the Bernie oppo book on behalf of the Clinton campaign. “One of the reasons we hired Tyson is to prepare this campaign for whatever false accusations and allegations are leveled against us,” Faiz Shakir, then Sanders’ campaign manager, told New York Magazine at the time. (Shakir did not respond to a request for comment for this story.)


Before his Substack went quiet, Brody detailed some of his basic approach, which involved obsessing over documents, carpet bombing public institutions with records requests and pitching the results to reporters, who, he wrote, were often uninterested. He described one such quest in 2014, when he served as research director on the ultimately losing campaign of then-Democratic Sen. Mary Landrieu: “There’s nothing as satisfying as finding something someone tried to hide, building a case brick by brick, and finally forcing it into the open. ... Ultimately the best oppo isn’t the fanciest detective work. It’s finding the words that let the voters say what they want to think.”


One of the things that distinguishes good oppo from merely OK oppo is persistence, said Rodota. He noted that Brody, via his Twitter feed, was prepared to shoot down the inevitable pushback and denials from the opposing campaign about the medical debt story. For instance, when Marshall’s campaign denied responsibility for charging patients 18% interest on their debt, Brody posted billing statements from Marshall’s own office detailing the interest rate. Seeing that, Rodota thought, “There’s somebody who has organized the material and is waiting for a rebuttal and is prepared.”


Throughout the fall, Marshall has faced a steady drip of damaging revelations, to the point that the campaign has launched a section of its webpage devoted to rebutting them. There was the Kansas Reflector and MSNOW story, based on documents the outlets “obtained” and linking to a Brody tweet in the very first sentence, raising questions about whether Marshall’s office was blurring the line between official and campaign spending. (The Marshall campaign’s site says the senator is fully compliant with FEC rules and has a campaign team separate from his official staff.) A few days later came an AP story describing an ultimately unsuccessful earmark Marshall requested that could boost the value of the senator’s own property. (A campaign spokesperson told the outlet the project would have benefited a wildlife refuge and not the property.) In between, there was the Facebook post Brody surfaced from the owner of a local bakery, who posted a $678.75 unpaid invoice from supplying baked goods to Marshall’s 2020 campaign — an episode Brody dubbed “#cookiegate” that eventually wound its way into The New York Times. (Marshall paid almost double the invoice after the bill became public, though not, as Brody pointed out, with 18% interest.) “It’s just kind of this ongoing, never-ending saga that has plagued Roger Marshall from the end of the primary on,” said All, the Democratic operative.


In the meantime, national Republicans have taken note to the extent that Trump himself descended on Kansas for a rally this week, where he defended Marshall by musing aloud that his critics were “making him look like a Shylock type guy” for attempting to collect his medical debts.


Brody gleefully tweeted the clip.

item.title: Met Police received claims about Meghan's father, but didn't share with other agencies
item.description:
Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, said she is "deeply distressed" by the news that her father, Thomas Markle, is under investigation over claims he possessed images containing child sexual abuse in his home.

The images were reportedly found in his home in the Philippines after he returned to the U.S. in May, Philippine officials said.

Thomas Markle denied the allegations, calling them "sick lies" and "the worst thing anyone could accuse me of."

London’s Metropolitan Police confirmed Saturday that it received a letter in January 2019 containing “a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom,” the BBC reported. The letter was sent to the force’s protection command because of concerns about the duchess’s security.

The Met said it passed the letter to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex “for their awareness,” but did not share the details with other law enforcement agencies. The force said it is reviewing how it handled the matter and considering whether to refer itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct, the police watchdog.

In a statement through her spokesperson, Meghan Markle said that she is "deeply distressed" by the news, and that she was first made aware of the claims by the Met Police in 2018.

"I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed," Meghan's statement said. "In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan police and Royalty and Specialist Protection. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father, and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.

"I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications' distortion over the years, any distance from my father, and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them.

"I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.

"Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children."

Meghan had said the letter was sent in 2018. A spokesman for the duchess said Saturday that “any discrepancy of a few months” was “an understandable consequence of that passage of time.”

Authorities in the Philippines are also investigating. Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said national police had secured Markle’s computer for a forensic examination, the BBC reported.

The allegations, reported by Mail Online, said Thomas Markle is under investigation after being reported by his son, Thomas Markle Jr. 

In a statement to Mail Online, the elder Markle said: "I'm shocked, I'm hurt and I'm very upset that my son is making these accusations against me. I could never do what I'm being accused of. It's the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.”

He added: "It's just a bunch of lies. It's sick. I have no idea why Tom [Markle] is trying to destroy me with these lies."

Yahoo has contacted the Met Office and authorities in the U.S. and the Philippines for comment. 

This article originally appeared on Yahoo News at https://www.yahoo.com/news/world/article/met-police-says-it-received-2019-letter-with-claims-about-meghans-father-but-didnt-share-it-with-other-agencies-163535130.html

item.title: DOJ charges government contractor with leaking secrets to journalist girlfriend
item.description:
By Daniel Trotta

Oct 23 (Reuters) - The US Justice Department accused a government contractor on Friday of leaking national defense information to his girlfriend, the publisher of a Substack newsletter.

The FBI arrested Ian Brinksman, ‌42, on Friday following a search of his Washington home, a Justice Department statement said. Prosecutors charged ‌him with unlawfully transmitting national defense information.

A federal public defender representing Brinksman declined to comment.

“As alleged, Brinksman reached far outside his own duties ​to obtain some of our Nation’s most closely held secrets and handed them to a romantic partner he knew intended to publish them,” John Eisenberg, assistant attorney general for national security, said in the statement.

“That is not carelessness. It is a betrayal of his oath and the American people who entrusted him to fulfill his duties honorably,” Eisenberg ‌said.

Brinksman held a top secret security clearance ⁠while working as an employee of a US government agency and later as a developer for systems integration for a private contractor working for the same agency, prosecutors said.

According ⁠to the sworn affidavit of an FBI agent investigating the case, Brinksman repeatedly accessed classified intelligence reports and then communicated with the journalist. The affidavit also cites phone records, database access logs, badge-swipe records, emails and other evidence.

The affidavit only ​identifies ​the journalist as "Individual 1," but it cites excerpts from articles ​she published.

"A fundraising article reportedly published by ‌Individual 1 in September 2026 stated 'over the past year (Individual 1 has) published reporting based on classified (relevant U.S. government agency) assessments that I believe the public deserves to know about,'" the affidavit reads.

That quote appears in a September 28 piece published on the Capital & Empire online newsletter authored by Aída Chávez.

"Over the past year, I’ve published reporting based on classified CIA assessments that I believe the public deserves to know about," wrote Chávez, whose profile on the site ‌notes that she worked for the Nation and other outlets ​before she launched the newsletter.

Chávez did not respond to an email ​message seeking comment.

Investigators allege that on at least ​five occasions in 2026, Individual 1 published Substack articles containing information that mirrored the classified reports, ‌some at the top secret level. On some ​of those dates, Chávez published ​articles that cite classified reports, some of them attributed to the CIA.

According to a LinkedIn profile bearing Brinksman's name, he worked for Deloitte as a manager and as a senior strategy security consultant after having ​worked as a US State Department ‌foreign service officer on dates corresponding to those outlined in the Justice Department statement.

The State Department ​declined to comment. Deloitte did not respond to requests for comment.

(Reporting by Daniel Trotta in Carlsbad, ​California; Editing by Tom Hogue, Sergio Non, Rod Nickel)

This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/us-accuses-government-contractor-leaking-025315584.html

item.title: A 30-year GOP losing streak hangs over Mike Rogers's bid for Michigan's Senate seat
item.description:
Mike Rogers and Abdul El-Sayed, the respective Republican and Democratic candidates in Michigan's crucial Senate race, sparred over tariffs, the Supreme Court, health care and a range of other issues in a contentious debate Wednesday night. 

Both candidates are jockeying for an edge in a tight matchup that's likely to play a significant role in deciding which party controls the upper chamber of Congress after the midterms. According to forecasters, Michigan may be the GOP's best opportunity to flip a blue Senate seat on Nov. 3, which could prove critical to maintaining its slim majority as Democrats target GOP incumbents in a number of red states across the country. 

Michigan hasn’t elected a Republican to the Senate in more than three decades, but Rogers came extremely close to ending that streak two years ago, and polls suggest he may have another chance this time around. 

Throughout the campaign, El-Sayed has garnered far more attention because of his progressive policy positions, a very competitive Democratic primary and the novelty of his emergence onto the national political stage. But Rogers is far from an also-ran. He has managed to keep this race tight at the same time as some other swing-state Republican candidates have lagged well behind their Democratic opponents. 

Here’s a guide to who Mike Rogers is, what he stands for and how strong his chances of turning Michigan’s Senate seat red appear to be. 

Who is Mike Rogers?

Rogers was born in Livingston County, Mich., in 1963. His father was a teacher and vice principal. His mother led the local chamber of commerce. He earned a bachelor’s degree in criminal justice and sociology from Adrian College in 1985 before joining the Army. 

After four years of military service, Rogers joined the FBI as a special agent based in Chicago. His work with federal law enforcement focused on countering organized crime and public corruption. Rogers began his political career in 1994, when he was elected to a seat in the Michigan state legislature. He served for six years before launching his first bid for Congress. 

Rogers was elected to the House of Representatives in one of the closest races of the 2000 election cycle, defeating Democrat Dianne Byrum by just 111 votes. During his 14-year tenure in the House, Rogers was a key conservative voice on national security and intelligence issues. He spent four years as chairman of the powerful House Intelligence Committee, much of that time focused on what he describes as “the economic and national security danger posed by China.” 

He was the primary sponsor of several bills centered on honoring public servants that ultimately became law, including legislation making it a crime to protest outside a fallen military member’s funeral at federal cemeteries and a bill that provided relocation assistance to families of federal law enforcement officers who die during their service. 

Rogers left Congress in 2015 and quickly began a career in media. He hosted a daily syndicated radio show called Something to Think About with Mike Rogers and worked as a commentator for CNN. He also had high-ranking roles in several tech and security companies during this period. 

He returned to politics in 2024, when he ran for an open Senate seat in Michigan. Once again, Rogers was involved in one of the nation’s tightest races, but this time he was on the wrong side. He was defeated by Democrat Elissa Slotkin by just 19,000 votes, losing by a margin of 0.34 percentage points. 

Roughly six months after that loss, Rogers announced his plan to run for the Senate again in 2026. After his early entry into the race, no other significant candidate joined the Republican primary, allowing him to run unopposed. 

Rogers has been married to his wife Kristi, a longtime executive in the security industry, since 2010. He has two adult children from a previous marriage. 

What does Rogers stand for?

Rogers is a conservative Republican on most issues. 

He is personally opposed to abortion, but has said he would vote against a national abortion ban if he were in the Senate, arguing that the issue should be left up to the states. He has been a longtime proponent of strict immigration laws and accused El-Sayed of advocating for “open borders.” 

While in Congress, he voted in favor of a proposed constitutional amendment banning same-sex marriage nationwide and opposed the repeal of the military’s “don’t ask, don’t tell” policy toward LGBTQ service members, though he said more recently that his views on LGBTQ rights have “evolved” over time. Like many Republicans this midterm cycle, he has come out strongly in opposition to transgender athletes participating in girls’ and women’s sports. 

Rogers’s opinion on President Trump has shifted through the years. After the 2020 presidential election, he denounced Trump’s efforts to overturn the results.

“Refusing to recognize state-certified elections without evidence of fraud is an abdication of the higher responsibility to our Constitution,” he wrote in an op-ed for the Washington Post published the day before the Jan. 6 assault on the U.S. Capitol. 

In 2022, he said he did not support the president’s ambition to run for a second term, saying, “Trump’s time has passed.”

During his two Senate campaigns, however, Rogers has spoken more favorably of the president, including echoing some of his unsubstantiated claims about widespread fraud in Michigan’s elections. Despite Rogers’s past criticisms, Trump has endorsed him in both races. 

In the later stages of this year’s campaign, Rogers has broken from Trump on two key issues: tariffs and the war in Iran. Over the past few weeks, Rogers has pulled back from his early support for Trump on both topics — calling for Trump to end the “tariff war” with Canada and saying the conflict in Iran should “end quickly.”

What are his chances?

Since the primary, polls have, on average, shown El-Sayed with a modest lead of about 3 percentage points, a small enough advantage to suggest that the race could go either way — particularly if polls are once again underestimating Republicans’ support as they have in some other recent elections. 

The Cook Political Report, one of the nation’s most respected election forecasters, lists the contest between Rogers and El-Sayed as a toss-up. Another highly regarded forecaster, the Center for Politics, classifies the race as “leans Democrat.”
